extracted.intended_audience: students of Catholic theology / theologians / seminarians
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating theological positions (Calvinism, Thomism, Molinism, Jansenism, etc.) concerning predestination, reprobation, grace, and free-will against Scripture, Tradition, and philosophical/theological coherence. Focused on whether a system preserves Church dogma and the moral attributes of God while avoiding logical contradictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with Revelation (Scripture)
rubrics_metrics.description: A doctrinal system must not run counter to texts of the Bible which assert the universality of God’s saving will, the bestowal of sufficient grace on all sinners, and the divine attribute of holiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text objects that Calvinism 'runs counter to all those texts of the Bible which assert the universality of God’s saving will, the bestowal of sufficient grace on all sinners, and the divine attribute of holiness.' Specific scriptural considerations include readings of Romans, 1 Peter, Isaiah VIII and Matthew XXI; appeal to passages such as 'wills not that any should perish, but that all should return to penance.' Use concordant scriptural passages to test any interpretation (misreadings like Beza’s of 1 Pet. II are criticized).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with Tradition (Fathers and Councils)
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine must accord with the teaching of the Fathers and Ecumenical Councils; patristic consensus (especially Eastern Fathers) is treated as a critical touchstone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page emphasizes unanimous patristic opposition to Calvinist determinations (with the one contested case of Augustine). Councils cited include the Second Council of Orange (condemning predestining some to evil) and the Tridentine Council (anathema against those who make grace restricted to the predestined). Use Fathers and Council declarations to evaluate theological claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not attribute sin or damnation to the will of God
rubrics_metrics.description: A correct doctrine must not assert that Adam’s sin, human ruin, or the condemnation of the reprobate are attributable solely to the will or positive decree of God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book quotes the Council of Orange and Tridentine definitions condemning views that predestine men to evil. Theological proposals that make God the author of sin or that posit a divine will to condemn are condemned as 'abominable' and 'anathema.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve human freedom of the will under efficacious grace
rubrics_metrics.description: The Church’s teaching upholds both the freedom of the will and the efficacy of grace — doctrines must preserve human liberty even under efficacious (not merely sufficient) grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Council of Trent is cited: denying the freedom of the will under divine excitation is anathema. The reformers (Luther, Calvin) and Jansenists who deny freedom under grace are explicitly criticized. Arguments must show how grace and freedom can coöperate (the text surveys Thomism, Molinism, Congruism, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain the universality of God’s salvific will
rubrics_metrics.description: A doctrine must not imply that God absolutely wills or determines some men to perish; it must preserve the sincerity of God’s will that all be saved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative reprobation and absolute predestination are criticized because they would make it metaphysically impossible for some to be saved, contradicting Revelation that God 'wills' salvation for all. Suarez’s attempts to reconcile this are judged insufficient. The moral character of God (love, justice) is part of the testing criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve a coherent notion of sufficient grace
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinction between 'gratia efficax' (efficacious grace) and 'gratia mere sufficiens' (sufficient grace) must not render 'sufficient grace' actually insufficient to perform the good it is said to enable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thomistic accounts that make sufficient grace require an additional intrinsic efficacious grace are criticized as making the notion of sufficiency incoherent. The page documents Thomist responses (Gazzaniga, De Lemos, Billuart) and the resultant logical difficulty; a viable system must avoid this paradox.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making God the author of sin through predetermination
rubrics_metrics.description: Theological formulations must not imply that God causally produces sinful acts or is the moral author of sin even while explaining divine causality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thomists insist 'God is not the author of sin' — He moves the sinner but does not move him to sin; malice derives from free will. Critiques focus on whether premotion/predetermination nevertheless makes God morally responsible. Any account of divine concurrence must safeguard against making God the author of sin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject a praedeterminatio ad unum that destroys freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrines positing an intrinsic 'praedeterminatio ad unum' (pre-determination to one outcome) that removes the will's capacity to choose are incompatible with the dogma of free-will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that a determinatio ad unum (physical premotion to a single act) implies a necessitas consequentis incompatible with genuine liberty. Thomistic distinctions (necessitas consequentiae vs. consequentis) are debated; an acceptable theory must avoid implying determinatio ad unum in a way that nullifies active indifference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not resolve intrinsic logical contradictions by appealing to omnipotence
rubrics_metrics.description: One must not cure metaphysical contradictions (e.g., a determinatio ad unum coexisting with genuine liberty) simply by appealing to God's omnipotence; intrinsic impossibilities remain unsolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text rebukes the Thomist move of saying God’s omnipotence makes predetermination compatible with freedom, arguing that intrinsic contradictions cannot be solved by omnipotence (analogy: God cannot make a square circle). Theological explanations must be philosophically coherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret scripture and patristic texts contextually; avoid simplistic literalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Scriptural passages and patristic statements must be read in context and balanced with other texts and traditions; isolated readings that produce deterministic conclusions are suspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Beza’s use of 1 Pet. II to claim persons are 'predestined not to believe' is criticized; other scriptures (Is. VIII, Matt. XXI) and patristic exegesis must be considered. The method of interpretation is itself a criterion for doctrinal soundness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make doctrinal distinctions substantive not merely evasive
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical distinctions introduced to defend liberty (e.g., sensus compositus vs. sensus divisus; potentia dissentiendi) must be real capacities, not verbal maneuvers that leave claimed powers powerless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Thomistic sensus compositus/divisus distinction is criticized as evasive; describing a 'potentia dissentiendi' that can never be active is judged not to secure true liberty. Distinctions must have explanatory force, not just dialectical form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid doctrines that ascribe cruel intentions to God
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral consequences of a doctrine (e.g., doctrines that imply God 'tries with all His might to prevent' some from attaining salvation) are a test: any teaching that makes God appear cruel or intentionally depriving is unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative reprobation is called 'heartless and cruel' when it implies God wills or devises means to prevent the salvation of some. The moral plausibility and pastoral consequences of doctrines are evaluated alongside doctrinal correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with explicit dogmatic declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: Any theological theory must not contradict explicit dogmatic decisions (e.g., Tridentine declarations such as 'there is no condemnation in those who are truly buried together with Christ by baptism').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text cites Tridentine anathemas and uses them to reject systems that imply otherwise; conformity with formal dogmatic pronouncements is decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance of multiple theological systems within legitimate bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: While the Church tolerates several speculative systems (Thomism, Molinism, Congruism, eclectic attempts), students should avoid preconceived opinions and not let intra-Church disputes distract from more pressing matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns students that the Church tolerates different systems and counsels prudence: 'the ancient controversy between Thomism and Molinism had better be left in abeyance' when greater threats to faith exist. The criterion here is pastoral prudence and recognition of legitimate theological diversity.
